passage: Our neighbours Siddharth and Indu sit at their balcony table most Sunday mornings with tea and a notebook, and this month I could not help overhearing. "If we start next year," Indu said, "who takes the leave, and for how long?" Siddharth counted on fingers. "My office is flexible for a few weeks. Yours is longer." They talked about rent, what would come out of the monthly spending, and who would do the night wakings. Siddharth asked, "And if we're not ready by then?" Indu said, "Then we say so and move the date." I do not know what either of them felt underneath. At one point Indu went quiet and looked at the road. But they were not guessing at what the other wanted. They were writing it down.

qa.q: Where do Siddharth and Indu usually sit to talk?
qa.a: At their balcony table on Sunday mornings, with tea and a notebook.

qa.q: What might Indu have been feeling when going quiet and looking at the road?
qa.a: Indu may have felt thoughtful or a little uncertain, though the narrator says they do not know what either felt underneath.

qa.q: What could the couple do if they find they are not ready by next year?
qa.a: They could move the date, as Indu says, and keep checking in together about leave, spending and night wakings.

qa.q: How does the narrator see the couple's approach?
qa.a: The narrator sees them treating the question as a joint plan rather than an assumption, since they talk through leave, money and night wakings and write it down.

grounding: A neighbour watches a couple talk through timing, leave, spending and who does what for a possible baby.

Saturday. Keerthana and Irfan had been married a year, and relatives kept asking about "good news". On a walk by the lake in Bhopal, Keerthana said, "Before anyone else decides, can we?" They agreed to talk properly, not in bits.
The next Tuesday. They sat with tea and four questions: When? Keerthana wanted to finish her certification first, about a year. Who takes leave, and how much? Irfan said he wanted to take real time off, not just a few days. What changes in spending? Less eating out, more saving. What worries each of them? Irfan admitted he was scared of not being good at it.
Two weeks later. They wrote their plan on one page: start trying after the certification, both take leave, begin a savings habit now. Keerthana stuck it inside the wardrobe door. "It's ours," she said.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana and Irfan walk on Saturday?

qa.a: Irfan was scared of not being good at being a parent.

qa.q: What else could Keerthana and Irfan add to their plan?
qa.a: They could check both employers' leave policies and, for health questions, book a general check-up with a doctor.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel about the one-page plan?
qa.a: Keerthana feels settled and in control, since the plan is theirs rather than something relatives decided.

grounding: It shows a couple discussing when to start a family, how leave will work, who takes time off and spending changes, treating it as a joint plan over several days.

Yamini, you and your husband are thinking about children? Let me, Zubin, your old grandfather, tell you how your grandmother and I did it, back in Bombay in 1975.
Back then, people just assumed. Get married, have a baby, the wife stays home. But your grandmother was a teacher and loved it.
So one evening on the Marine Drive wall, she said, "Zubin, let's not assume. Let's decide." We talked for three evenings. When? After she finished her B.Ed., two years later. Who would take time off? She would take her leave, and I'd come home by six every day, no excuses. Money? I stopped smoking and put that money aside. What scared us? Her: losing her work. Me: not earning enough.
Your father came along in 1977. Your grandmother went back to teaching after a year.
We didn't assume, Yamini. We planned together. That's why it worked.

qa.q: What year was Yamini's father born?
What were Zubin and his wife each afraid of?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing her work, and Zubin was afraid of not earning enough.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zubin's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The turning point was the evening on the Marine Drive wall when she said, "Let's not assume"; it led them to plan timing, leave and money together instead of following custom.

qa.q: How might Zubin's wife have felt about the plan they made?
qa.a: She likely felt respected and relieved, since her teaching career was part of the plan rather than assumed away.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he and his wife discussed timing, leave, roles and spending before starting a family, treating it as a joint plan.
